rationale: A wins because it gives the founder four genuinely different reporting doors and keeps the missing proof visible instead of decorating around it. Its best headline, "Replit says anyone can build an app with plain English. It won't say how often those apps actually work," is a clean accountability story anchored in the supplied facts. B has good instincts, but "Replit contradicting its own founding premise" is the kind of confident flourish that makes a reporter ask for the fact you do not have.
gaps_in_A: "huge, largely non-technical user base" is not supplied. The update says Replit has tens of millions of users and positions the agent for non-engineers; it does not prove the existing user base is largely non-technical.
"betting its core product" overstates strategy. A launch is not evidence that the whole company has reorganized around this agent.
"shadow IT, AppSec, and unmanaged software sprawl" is a plausible security lens, but it needs testing or company guardrail detail before it stops being a smart worry and becomes a pitchable story.
gaps_in_B: "Replit contradicting its own founding premise" is invented. The update says Replit is used heavily in education, not what its founding premise was.
"built its user base ... on ... learning to code" stretches the facts. Heavy education use does not support a claim about the whole user base or company identity.

"the market has moved from AI that assists developers to AI that replaces the development workflow" turns one Replit launch into a market conclusion. The set admits it needs comparable offerings, which means the angle is underproved as written.
